title: Hook
text: What happens to your body if you suddenly fall out of an airplane at ten thousand meters? The first enemy is not the ground rushing toward you.
nxt: It is the cold, thin air itself. And yet history records a handful of people who fell from this height and lived.

title: Thin Air
text: At ten kilometers up, the air pressure is only about a quarter of what it is at sea level.
nxt: With so little oxygen reaching your blood, an ordinary person has roughly thirty seconds, sometimes even less, of useful consciousness.

title: Cold
text: Then comes the cold. The air temperature at this height is typically around minus fifty degrees Celsius, and the wind rushing past your skin strips away heat.
nxt: Without protective gear, frostbite can begin within minutes.

title: Drag
text: Meanwhile, you are falling. At first you speed up at nine point eight meters per second squared. But the air pushes back.
nxt: The faster you fall, the more air you slam into, and the stronger the drag becomes.

title: Drag

nxt: Soon the upward drag matches the downward pull of gravity, and you stop speeding up.

title: Terminal Velocity
text: That steady speed is called terminal velocity. In the thin air up high, it can briefly top three hundred kilometers per hour.
nxt: Lower down, where the air is thicker, it settles at roughly two hundred kilometers per hour.

title: The Landing Problem
text: Surviving the fall is not the real question. The real question is the stop.
nxt: Concrete, asphalt, and solid rock stop a body over a few millimeters, and bones and organs cannot take that force.

title: Soft Stops
text: The accounts of survivors point to surfaces that give way.
nxt: A dense forest canopy can act as a multi-stage brake, as twigs snap and thicker branches bend and break.

title: Soft Stops

title: Water Warning
text: What about water? It feels like the soft choice, but at two hundred kilometers per hour, water is almost incompressible and cannot get out of the way fast enough.
nxt: It can behave much like a hard surface, and hitting it flat-on is very often fatal.
